issues.legal_issue: A statutory power to exempt buildings from rent-control protections is not an excessive delegation when the legislation provides sufficient guidance for its exercise.
material_facts: The tenants challenged the statutory provision authorising the government to exempt a building or class of buildings from all or any of the rent-control law.
The statutory preamble and operative provisions identified the law’s purposes and provided guidance for deciding when exemptions could be granted.
The challenge to the provision was not pressed in light of an earlier decision concerning an identical provision in an earlier enactment.
issues.conclusion: The statutory exemption power does not suffer from excessive delegation and is not invalid under the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a statutory delegation is sufficiently guided where the legislation’s preamble and operative provisions indicate the policy and purposes governing the discretion. The power to grant exceptions may address undue hardship or abuse arising from uniform application, but must not subvert the enactment’s general purpose. P.J. Irani v. State of Madras upheld an identical exemption power on this basis; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kanhaiyalal likewise upheld a guided exemption power.

predicates.rent_control_delegation_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law that authorises the government to exempt buildings from rent-control protections.
predicates.statutory_scheme_supplies_guidance: The legislation’s stated purposes and operative scheme guide the government in deciding when exemptions may be granted.

issues.definition: When a rent-control delegation challenge concerns an exemption power guided by the legislation’s purposes and scheme, the delegation is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: An exemption for buildings owned by public religious and charitable trusts satisfies equal protection when the class is distinct and the exemption has a rational connection to the purpose of the exemption power.
material_facts: Tenants challenged a notification exempting buildings owned by public religious trusts and public charitable trusts from all provisions of the rent-control law.

Public religious and charitable trusts served public purposes, and the use of their income was governed by the purposes for which they were created, distinguishing their buildings from those of private landlords.

The government stated in affidavits that rents paid by tenants were very low, statutory fair-rent fixation would not meet the needs of the trusts, and tenants were exploiting the trusts’ situation and helplessness.
The tenants filed no rejoinder affidavits disputing the government’s account.
issues.conclusion: The classification was based on an intelligible differentia and had a rational connection to relieving hardship arising from the uniform application of the rent-control law; the exemption did not violate equal protection.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification based on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus with the relevant statutory purpose. The exemption power must be exercised consistently with the rent-control law’s policy, including relief from undue hardship or abuse of its protections. P.J. Irani v. State of Madras recognised that a class of buildings belonging to charitable or religious bodies could be rationally distinguished. State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kanhaiyalal illustrates that the government must consider grounds germane to the law’s purpose; State of Rajasthan v. Mukanchand was inapplicable because the classification here had the required nexus.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge_to_exemption_: The proceeding challenges on equal-protection grounds a government notification exempting a class of buildings from rent-control protections.
predicates.public_endowment_owners: The exempted buildings are owned by public religious or charitable bodies whose income is applied according to their public purposes.
predicates.distinct_public_purpose_and_income_const: The owners’ public functions and constraints on use of their income distinguish them from ordinary private landlords.
predicates.unchallenged_evidence_of_inadequate_rent: The government presents evidence that protected rents are inadequate and uniform application of rent-control protections causes hardship to the owners, and the challengers do not dispute that evidence.

issues.definition: When an equal-protection challenge concerns an exemption for distinct public-purpose owners and undisputed evidence shows inadequate rents and resulting hardship, the class exemption satisfies equal protection.

issues.legal_issue: A total exemption from rent-control protections is not excessive when rent control and eviction restrictions operate together and the circumstances support giving the exempted owners effective freedom to obtain reasonable rent and recover possession.
material_facts: The notification exempted buildings owned by public religious and charitable trusts from all provisions of the rent-control law.
The government considered the statutory fair rents unjustly low for those buildings and sought to allow the trusts to recover reasonable market rent.

The court treated rent control and restrictions on eviction as interrelated, reasoning that the ability to recover market rent would be ineffective if tenants could not be evicted for failing to pay it.
The trusts might also need possession to carry out major repairs or demolition and reconstruction.
issues.conclusion: The total exemption was not excessive or unwarranted; the choice between partial and total exemption was for the government to make in light of the statutory scheme and the circumstances, provided the exemption was not illegal or unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: The objectives of controlling rent and preventing unreasonable eviction are interrelated, and provisions serving those objectives supplement each other. P.J. Irani v. State of Madras described those objectives as intertwined. An effective ability to charge reasonable market rent may require an ability to recover possession for non-payment, and possession may also be needed for substantial repairs or reconstruction. The extent and conditions of an exemption are for the government to determine in light of the legislation and the circumstances, subject to constitutional and legal limits.

predicates.challenge_to_total_rent_control_exemptio: The proceeding challenges a government decision to exempt a class of buildings from all rent-control protections rather than only some of them.
predicates.rent_and_eviction_controls_are_interrela: The protections controlling rent and restricting eviction operate together to achieve the law’s objectives.
predicates.owners_need_effective_market_rent_recove: The owners need a practical ability to recover reasonable market rent, including possession where tenants do not pay it.
predicates.possession_may_be_needed_for_substantial: The owners may need possession to carry out substantial repairs, demolition, or reconstruction.

issues.definition: When a total-exemption challenge concerns interrelated rent and eviction controls, effective market-rent recovery, and possible need for possession for substantial work, the total exemption is not excessive.
